Reading the rings: denominators and unidentified prey

Source: vignettes/articles/within-rank-na.Rmd
within-rank-na.Rmd

A DietView sunburst shows the diet at seven ranks at once, from kingdom at the center to species at the edge. This article explains what a percentage in any ring is a percentage of, and why prey that could not be identified to a given rank stay in the figure instead of being dropped. It uses the invented example table that ships with the package (24 prey records from 11 stomachs), so the numbers illustrate the bookkeeping, not the diet of these fish.

library(DietView)

dat <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "dietview_example.csv", package = "DietView"),
                na.strings = c("NA", ""))
lin <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "dietview_example_lineage.csv", package = "DietView"),
                na.strings = c("NA", ""))
spec <- dv_spec(predator = "predator_species_common_name", stomach = "stomach_id",
                prey_id = "aphia_id", prey_name = "verified_name",
                weight = "prey_weight", digestion = "digestion_level_id")
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = lin, verbose = FALSE)
tree <- dv_build_tree(prep$data, prep$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight)

One record, one place in every ring

dv_build_tree() gives every record one place at every rank: the taxon it was identified to at that rank or, if identification stopped earlier, an unidentified node (NA in the tables) below the last rank it reached. A shrimp named Pandalus borealis sits under Decapoda at order and under Pandalus at genus. A record named only “Decapoda” sits under Decapoda at order and in the unidentified node below Decapoda at family, genus and species.

So every ring holds the same records and the same weight:

rings <- unique(tree$rank)
data.frame(
  rank      = rings,
  records   = sapply(rings, function(r) sum(tree$value_occ[tree$rank == r])),
  weight_g  = sapply(rings, function(r) round(sum(tree$value_w[tree$rank == r]), 1)),
  pct_total = sapply(rings, function(r) round(sum(tree$pct_occ[tree$rank == r]), 1)),
  row.names = NULL
)
#>      rank records weight_g pct_total
#> 1 Kingdom      24     77.2       100
#> 2  Phylum      24     77.2       100
#> 3   Class      24     77.2       100
#> 4   Order      24     77.2       100
#> 5  Family      24     77.2       100
#> 6   Genus      24     77.2       100
#> 7 Species      24     77.2       100

Each percentage in the tree (pct_occ for records, pct_w for weight) is a node’s value divided by that common total, and each ring adds up to 100%. Because no record is lost between rings, a node’s value is also the sum of its children’s values, which is what lets the rings nest:

kids <- tapply(tree$value_occ, tree$parent, sum)
parents <- tree[tree$id %in% names(kids), ]
all.equal(parents$value_occ, as.numeric(kids[parents$id]))
#> [1] TRUE

What dropping the unidentified records would do

The usual alternative is to drop, at each rank, the records that were not identified to that rank, and to compute shares among the rest. Each ring then has its own total, and the rings stop agreeing with each other:

id_only <- function(r) tree[tree$rank == r & tree$label != "NA", ]
cl <- id_only("Class"); od <- id_only("Order")
mal_class <- 100 * sum(cl$value_occ[cl$label == "Malacostraca"]) / sum(cl$value_occ)
mal_order <- 100 * sum(od$value_occ[grepl("|Malacostraca|", od$id, fixed = TRUE)]) /
             sum(od$value_occ)
round(c(class_ring = mal_class, order_ring = mal_order), 1)
#> class_ring order_ring 
#>       50.0       73.3

Malacostraca would be 50% of the identified records at class, while its three orders together would be 73.3% of the identified records at order. Nothing about the diet changed between the two rings; only the set of records did. With the unidentified records kept, Malacostraca and its orders hold the same 11 records in both rings.

How much was not identified

dv_rank_table() lists one ring. At order, there is one unidentified row per parent: under Bivalvia, Polychaeta, Copepoda and the fish class, plus the material that could not be placed at all.

ord <- dv_rank_table(tree, "Order")
ord[ord$label == "NA", ]
#>    label value_item value_occ  pct_occ value_w        pct_w
#> 14    NA          1         2 8.333333  0.7030  0.910659509
#> 16    NA          1         2 8.333333  0.0018  0.002331703
#> 23    NA          1         2 8.333333  0.0290  0.037566324
#> 24    NA          1         2 8.333333  1.6000  2.072624772
#> 22    NA          1         1 4.166667  8.0000 10.363123860
sum(ord$pct_occ[ord$label == "NA"])
#> [1] 37.5

Here 37.5% of the records are unidentified at order. Report that figure next to any statement made at that rank: an order-level description of this diet rests on the remaining 62.5%.

The figures

Records first, then weight. The two currencies often rank prey differently, so look at both before choosing one to report.

dv_sunburst(tree, mode = "occurrence", title = "All predators",
            subtitle = "share of prey records")
dv_sunburst(tree, mode = "weight", title = "All predators",
            subtitle = "share of prey weight")

White wedges with gray edges are records not identified at that rank. Hovering over a wedge shows its count and its share of the ring.

Colors

dv_palette() gives each taxon name one color and unidentified nodes white. Build it once from all the records and pass it to every figure you want to compare, so the same taxon has the same color everywhere:

pal <- dv_palette(tree$label)
head(pal)
#>   Animalia   Annelida Arthropoda   Chordata   Mollusca Polychaeta 
#>  "#1f77b4"  "#aec7e8"  "#ff7f0e"  "#ffbb78"  "#2ca02c"  "#98df8a"

The palette has 20 colors and reuses them when there are more taxa, so in a large survey two taxa can share a color. Check the hover labels before you read a color as a taxon.

dv_palette_tree() is the alternative for large surveys. It gives one hue to each phylum (the second rank) and lighter tints of that hue to its descendants, and keeps unidentified nodes white. Its colors are keyed by node, so build it from the pooled tree and pass it to every panel in the same way:

pal_tree <- dv_palette_tree(tree)
dv_sunburst(tree, mode = "occurrence", colors = pal_tree, title = "All predators",
            subtitle = "share of prey records, colors by phylum")
